The reason why Scitools Understand, Depends and Titan are snapshot oriented in regards to SDSM. So I am just curious how they scalated this to every single commit for large project histories.

# Wolfgang MBOX Downloader

```
BASE_URL=http://mail-archives.apache.org/mod_mbox
PROJECT=hbase-dev
FROM=2015
TO=2020

for year in `seq ${FROM} ${TO}`; do
  for month in `seq -w 1 12`; do
     curl -s -I ${BASE_URL}/${PROJECT}/${year}${month}.mbox | \
          grep "HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found" > /dev/null || \
     curl ${BASE_URL}/${PROJECT}/${year}${month}.mbox \
          -o ${PROJECT}_${year}_${month}.mbox
  done
done

cat *.mbox > ${PROJECT}.mbox
rm ${PROJECT}_*.mbox
````

The net result is that a resource that should require a valid client certificate in order to get access can be accessed without that credential. Background: - ----------- Apache can control access to resources based on various things; such as a password, IP address and so on. One of the options, when SSL or TLS is used, is gating access based on the client having access to a private-key of a X509 client certificate. These client certificates are typically held on a chipcard (e.g. the CAC card in the US, national identity, banking cards or, for example, medical-chip cards in Europe). In some cases they are 'soft tokens' - i.e. files, often called PKCS#12 files, which are loaded into the browser or the 'keychain'. Gating access based on a client certificate is done by adding a line such as SSLVerifyClient require to the httpd configuration; along with a list of trusted client certificate authorities (SSLCACertificateFile). The commit 224a729 does the time-consuming task of figuring out percerval necessary flags to load the data into R via a json interface. Indeed, in the future a single .R file can just load the function created, to parse Perceval or output a network file would be trivial with the designed function.  

Pain points to create the function:

## 1.1 Percerval Git URI is misleading 

The Git_URI parameter required by Percerval is confusing, as it only uses to identify the git log. Virtually anything goes, but the interface makes it look like it requires both gitlog and repo, [which is not true](https://github.com/chaoss/grimoirelab-perceval/issues/99). The function abstracts the URI parameter, by using as convention the path to the repo (minus the `.git`) as an ID.  

## 1.2 R system calls 

There are 2 functions to run a command on unix from R. `system` and `system2`. Took me some time to make sense of `system2` interface, as it is not compatible with `system`. 

## 1.3 R parser of JSON is not trivial

Long story short, Percerval output files in a format where it line is a file. This is a common format for NoSQL dumps. R, on the other side, expects a connection to a database for this format. I have just a big text string instead. The workaround was found buried on an issue of the R package jsonlite used to parse Jsons into R. See here for [the details](https://github.com/jeroen/jsonlite/issues/59#issuecomment-308048597). 

The good news is that, all 3 pain points are abstracted by the function, as exemplified on the README.md. 

## Next steps 

Create an issue for network output from json, and one to calculate churn.
Note the communication network here is an **author-thread**. For metric purposes, a projection transformation is needed. I will do this in another issue.

The second motivation to go OO in my head, is to define clear interfaces to clarify Kaiaulu is not heavily dependent on any GPL licensed code. In essence, provided Kaiaulu has abstract classes, and various instance classes are instantiated from parsing **via terminal** data from GPL code (e.g. Perceval), then this codebase is free to be licensed as we see fit. 

Let me elaborate based on my IANAL musings:

# Licensing 

In the long run, I would like to make this code available publicly. I spent a bit of time reading on licensing again and found out R is actually mostly GPL. This is really restrictive for reuse from DV8, NASA, or anything else we want in the future. Instead, I think the MPL v2.0 (a bit more permissive than LGPL) license to be more aligned to my expectations here, while not throwing it to the wind like MIT and Apache.  

Specifically, here is the big big problem: Because R is interactive, calling `library (someGPLpackage)` actually, license wise, forces the entire code base to be GPL from IANAL advice I saw, [some people even left R due to it](https://www.r-bloggers.com/how-gpl-makes-me-leave-r-for-python/). 

Julia, the MIT language that came out to compete with Python and R for Data Science, for example, prefers, well, [the way more permissive MIT Licensing](https://discourse.julialang.org/t/gpl-and-virality/7715/12) --- Which I am actually not comfortable with.

Then there is data.table, which changed from [GPL to MPL 2.0](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/pull/2456), a package I use extensively in Kaiaulu, and their reasoning really resonates with me:

> I believed that closed-source products can already call interpreted R code, such as :

> library(data.table)
> DT = fread(...)
> DT[...]

> It was never our intention to prevent usage like that by closed-source products. I believed that R code was "data" and not considered linking.

> So, it is my new understanding that data.table's GPL license could be interpreted as preventing closed-source products from using data.table, even at R-only level. However strange that sounds, I'm willing to agree to that definition, for the avoidance of doubt.

> What we intended was that we contributed free software in the open under one condition: that if you improve data.table itself and distribute your improved data.table as a product, then that product must be open-source too. We were concerned about the code inside data.table itself, not use of data.table. **This is why, for data.table, we never agreed with MIT or Apache, and still don't. We do not like those licenses for data.table because we think them unfair to the contributors. We are concerned about, say, data.table.PRO, a closed-source improvement of data.table being created based on our free contributions. We are not concerned about using data.table as a library by closed-source software. In fact, we are now concerned about that being perceived as prevented**.

So what does that to do with adopting OO-R6 (which is MIT so safe)? According to what I read of GPL, if you call a GPL via terminal, as it is done here:

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/77f0d667aba9a316734407d70c58152b8e5a2958/R/parsers.R#L1-L31

Then even GPL is OK to not claim your codebase should be, by law, GPL (note, Perceval is also GPL). However, GPL also seems to have a clause where even if this is done, but your code is heavily shaped after the structure of the code, by law, it could be argued your code has to be GPL. 

Hence, if Kaiaulu has a clearly defined abstract interface (class R6) where it is clear Perceval is one of many other tools that could be used to extract git logs, there should be no doubt. 

Unfortunately, igraph is also GPL, and it is currently used in a Vignette to showcase the plots. Defining a class that simply obtains an edgelist in the format compatible with igraph, rather than output the igraph object itself seems to be a way to remove the igraph dependence, and leave Kaiaulu free to choose a license. 

While data.table is extensively used in Kaiaulu, it's permissive MPL 2.0 license would allow me to choose any license I like (since I don't have code from data.table pasted around). With that being said, I do believe we should license this code with `MPL.2.0` for the same reason: Code that improve this code base should belong in this repo. Code that uses, even via R as a library this package, can be closed source, or paid. It's a good middle ground between the two worlds, pending any further non IANAL clarification.

The reason why when computing architectural flaws we have to use `git checkout` given a `commit happens`, is because even though we may know a given commit only changed, say, 4 files, we do not know by just looking these 4 files the new dependencies it created to the rest of the codebase. Specifically, without using an abstract syntax tree, which in itself adds also another overhead, we have no means to know all types of dependencies (eg. inheritances) generated to any of the other files in the codebase, even if only those 4 files changed. Hence, we must perform git_checkout, and then analyze all the files. Tools, like Understand and Depends, will require a folder path and will not leverage the git commit because of that. A side effect is that most publications, if not all, will compute these metrics per time window, or per release rather than per commit as the cost is prohibitive.

Codeface does this across 3 files and a number of functions:

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/VCS.py#L1370

The ectags command is here: 

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/VCS.py#L1375-L1376 

For a given file, it will eventually set as part of a class instance what are the function definition lines are:

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/VCS.py#L1475 

Following the definition of Codeface's function `setFuncLines` to another file reveals the lines are considered also the "FuncIds" (note parameter renaming): 

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/fileCommit.py#L156

Knowing the file being analyzed function definitions starting line is called the function ids of the file now leads to Codeface's function `findFuncId` making sense, in particular, the use of [bisect_right](https://docs.python.org/2/library/bisect.html):

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/fileCommit.py#L173-L184

I.e. given a file, and knowing where each function definition line starts and without knowing where their definition ends, **codeface assumes all lines after a given function definition A start and before the next function definition, B starts, pertain to the function A (this is done via bisect). https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/VCS.py#L1455-L1469

As for the lapply:

```
for(i in window){
...loop that generates slicestack and calculates smells...
}
```

Ideally, we should actually remove the smells from this loop too. To be more precise, right now some of the quality metrics, such as `num.tz`, number of developers, etc are also in this loop. They should be outside, each as a function, since each takes as input a git log slice, a mailing list slice, or both. To be even more precise, let's look at the code in question:

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/2486a1a5d775e1338de20980266c67b52df23db3/vignettes/social_smells_showcase.Rmd#L173-L215

Right now, we have a list of time intervals we loop over, and at each step both git log and mailing list get subset to generate the slices. This should likely be turned into a function, which outputs the slices as a list. This function should likely be similar to how `identity_match()` input is like: You take as input a list of tables, that are guaranteed to have certain columns defined. In the case of identity match, those are the name and e-mail of users. That way, in the future, if we want to add, say, an issue tracker as a replacement or as an extra to mailing list, the function can accommodate it as an additional table to the passed list.

The same problem is true here: Right now to compute social smells we may either need a gitlog, a mailing list, or both. In the future, we may also want to use an issue tracker as a source of communication, much like the identity match. So again, passing a list of tables is likely the way to go. I hope you see the analogy in both concept and code here.

Now, contrary to identity match which purpose is just to perform identity match, we will want here to calculate multiple metrics of the tables passed in. 

Concerning this: 

```r
quality1 <- lappy(slicestack, quality_function1)
quality2 <- lappy(slicestack, quality_function2)
```

we will likely need something like this instead:

```{r}
quality_metrics <- lapply(slicestack,some_function,smell_and_quality_functions_stack)
```

Otherwise, we will have to loop over the slices times the number of metrics used. Since this number is large, and since projects like OpenSSL can be as long as 20 years, this can nuke the performance. So we want to still do it as much as possible in fewer loops, much not make a 3000 line loop which is hard to maintain. 

Note this is where it requires more thought about how to implement the turnover, since you need both the "current slice" as well as the "past slice". This is trivial in a for loop, since you can just `i` and `i-1`, but this is not that obvious in an lapply. And this is why exactly I've been slacking on coming out with a better way to modularize this.  

Whatever is chosen, this code should also be refactored into functions that can be used: 

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/2486a1a5d775e1338de20980266c67b52df23db3/vignettes/social_smells_showcase.Rmd#L266-L281

There is one more small thing I should point out, that may impact your analysis. Consider that, each slice of 3 months (or the slice of the time window you choose) subsets separately the git log and mailing list. It is unlikely on a large project, but it is possible one of the 4 cases occur:

 * No gitlog data is found, if no file changes happened in 3 months
 * No mailing list data is found, if no communication happened in 3 months
 * Both gitlog and mailing list had activity
 * Neither had activity

In the code I wrote, which is similar to the one you are thinking of now, the slices were smaller, since I looked at them "per project issue", and these 4 case types appeared much more often. This in turn can make a smell to not being computed for certain slices, if it requires the gitlog, mailing list, or both. Whatever function we come up with to iterate and compute these, has to account for that.
